books.title: The Way We Live Now
books.author: Anthony Trollope
books.desc: A mysterious financier dazzles London society with his schemes, while aristocrats, journalists and suitors chase money and advantage around him.
about: Augustus Melmotte, a financier of uncertain origins, arrives in London and quickly becomes the most talked-about man in the city, attracting investors and noble directors to a scheme for a great American railway. Around him circle Lady Carbury, a widow who writes books to support her spendthrift son Sir Felix; Felix himself, who courts Melmotte's daughter Marie for her fortune; Lady Carbury's daughter Hetta, torn between her cousin Roger Carbury and the young engineer Paul Montague; and Mrs Hurtle, an American woman from Paul's past.

Trollope's long novel is a broad satire of the greed and dishonesty he saw in English commercial, political and literary life, and of the new power of speculative finance. Its portraits of Melmotte and of the Jewish banker Brehgert reflect the antisemitic attitudes of its time.
The novel was inspired by the financial scandals of the early 1870s. It was first published in twenty monthly parts from February 1874 to September 1875, and in book form by Chapman and Hall in 1875.

books.title: McTeague
books.author: Frank Norris
books.desc: A slow-witted San Francisco dentist marries a young woman who wins a lottery, and greed gradually destroys everyone around them.
about: McTeague, a huge and simple former miner, runs a dental parlour on Polk Street in San Francisco. His friend Marcus Schouler brings his cousin Trina Sieppe to him for treatment, and McTeague falls in love with her. Soon after their engagement Trina wins five thousand dollars in a lottery. As the couple settle into married life among neighbours such as old Mr Grannis, who keeps a small dog hospital, the shy Miss Baker, the junk dealer Zerkow and the servant Maria Macapa, money, jealousy and resentment begin to take hold.

McTeague is a classic of American naturalism: Norris sought to show how heredity, environment and greed shape and degrade human lives. The novel's portrait of Zerkow draws on antisemitic stereotypes of its time.
McTeague was published in 1899. It was adapted for the cinema as McTeague (1916) and as Erich von Stroheim's Greed (1924).
books.author_short: American novelist (1870–1902), the first important naturalist writer in the United States, author of McTeague and The Octopus.
author_long: Frank Norris was born in Chicago on 5 March 1870. He studied art at the Académie Julian in Paris, then attended the University of California, Berkeley, and Harvard University, and worked as a news correspondent. He died of appendicitis in San Francisco on 25 October 1902, aged 32.

His novels include McTeague: A Story of San Francisco (1899), The Octopus: A Story of California (1901) and The Pit (1903), published after his death. The Octopus and The Pit were the first two parts of a planned trilogy, The Epic of the Wheat.

books.title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow
books.author: Washington Irving
books.desc: In a sleepy Dutch valley on the Hudson, a lanky schoolmaster courts a rich farmer's daughter and meets a ghostly Headless Horseman.
about: Around 1790, in the quiet glen of Sleepy Hollow near the Dutch settlement of Tarry Town on the Hudson, the people love ghost stories, above all the tale of a Headless Horseman. The bookish and superstitious schoolmaster Ichabod Crane hopes to win the hand of Katrina Van Tassel, the daughter of a wealthy farmer, but he has a rival in the strong and mischievous Brom Bones. One autumn night, after a party at the Van Tassels', Ichabod rides home alone.

Irving's tale mixes humour, local folklore and the supernatural, and offers an affectionate, ironic picture of the old Dutch communities of New York. The story is presented as found among the papers of the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker.

The Legend of Sleepy Hollow appeared in 1820 in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., a collection of essays and stories that Irving published in instalments in 1819 and 1820 under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon. He wrote it while living in Birmingham, England.
books.author_short: American writer and diplomat (1783–1859), author of Rip Van Winkle and The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.
author_long: Washington Irving was born in New York on 3 April 1783. He was a short-story writer, essayist, biographer and historian, and also served as United States minister to Spain under President John Tyler. He spent his later years at Sunnyside, his home near Tarrytown, New York, and died on 28 November 1859.

His best-known works are the stories Rip Van Winkle (1819) and The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (1820), both from The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. He wrote under several pen names, among them Geoffrey Crayon and Diedrich Knickerbocker.

books.title: Life on the Mississippi
books.author: Mark Twain
books.desc: Mark Twain recalls his years as a young steamboat pilot on the Mississippi and returns to the great river more than twenty years later.
about: Twain begins with the history of the Mississippi and his boyhood dream of working on the river. He then tells how, as a young man before the Civil War, he persuaded the experienced pilot Horace Bixby to take him on as a "cub" and learned to read the ever-changing river. In the second part he describes a journey made many years later by steamboat from St Louis to New Orleans and later on the upper river, observing how the towns and the river trade have changed.
Part memoir and part travel book, it mixes humour, tall tales, history and description. Some passages use the racial language and attitudes of its time towards Black and Native Americans.
The chapters on Twain's apprenticeship first appeared as "Old Times on the Mississippi" in The Atlantic Monthly. The complete book was published in 1883.

books.title: Little Lord Fauntleroy
books.author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
books.desc: A kind-hearted boy from New York learns he is heir to an English earldom and goes to live with his stern grandfather in a castle.
about: Cedric Errol lives modestly in New York with his widowed mother, whom he calls "Dearest", and his friends include Mr Hobbs the grocer and Dick the bootblack. One day a lawyer, Mr Havisham, arrives with news from England: Cedric's grandfather, the Earl of Dorincourt, who had disowned his son for marrying an American, has lost all his sons, and Cedric is now Lord Fauntleroy, heir to the title and a great estate. He travels to England to live with the old earl, a proud and bitter man.
Burnett's story contrasts the boy's open, generous nature with the selfishness of the aristocratic grandfather, and shows the power of kindness to change those around it.

Little Lord Fauntleroy was published as a serial in St. Nicholas Magazine from November 1885 to October 1886, then as a book by Scribner's in New York in 1886, with illustrations by Reginald Birch. In these illustrations and in the stage play that followed, Cedric wears long curls, velvet knee breeches and a lace collar, later known as a "Lord Fauntleroy collar".
